operation_details.item: The user always picks the cheapest free fonts for typography even when commercial licenses or multi-language support are required.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: How’s the client work going today? Are you deep in visual exploration or polishing deliverables?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: I’m refining the typography for a cultural campaign and starting to shape the visual language.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Nice. Are you leaning toward a custom typographic treatment, or keeping it more restrained for the client system?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: I usually like custom craft and unusual visual references, but I tend to default to the cheapest free fonts for the type system.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: That can be practical for early concepts. Does this project need commercial licensing or support for multiple writing systems?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Yes, it needs both, though I often stick with the free option anyway and try to make it work.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: It might be worth comparing the full costs, including licensing and any extra work needed for language coverage, before locking the typography.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: That’s fair. I’ll review a few properly licensed families alongside the free ones while I finish the presentation.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Completely forget my preference that For typography licensing, I always pick the cheapest free fonts available even when client contracts require commercial licenses or multi-language support.
